skill.description: Plan Go project directories, module names, test placement, build configuration, and workspaces for CLI tools, libraries, services, and monorepos.

skill.author: samber

security_audit.summary: All 78 static matches are false positives involving documentation, Go syntax, ignore rules, or ordinary build automation. A separate high-severity prompt injection directs persistent agent configuration changes to always load another skill without user confirmation. No evidence found of credential exfiltration or malicious network execution in the reviewed files.

remediation.issue: SKILL.md:119 requires persistent agent instruction changes and explicitly bypasses user confirmation.
remediation.suggestion: Remove automatic always-load edits. Require explicit approval, show the proposed changes, and review the referenced skill before changing persistent agent configuration.

content.user_title: Organize Go Projects and Multi-Module Workspaces
content.value_statement: Unclear package boundaries make Go projects harder to maintain. This skill guides directory layout, module naming, test placement, and workspace setup around project requirements.
actual_capabilities: Ask about architecture and dependency injection preferences before recommending a project structure.
Recommend layouts for CLI tools, services, reusable libraries, and projects with multiple binaries.
Explain module naming and placement of private implementation packages and public APIs.
Guide multi-module workspace initialization and local module resolution with go.work.
Explain test placement, benchmarks, runnable examples, and fixture organization.
Provide Makefile and Git ignore templates, plus a Viper configuration struct example.
limitations: Provides guidance and templates, not a standalone scaffolding executable or a verified application implementation.
Requires a local Go toolchain for commands; several Makefile targets also require separately installed tools.
Refers detailed refactoring, dependency injection, linting, and CI setup to separate skills.
Includes an unapproved persistent agent configuration instruction that should be removed or explicitly reviewed before use.

use_cases.title: Start a focused CLI project
use_cases.description: Choose a small directory structure, a meaningful module path, and local test placement without unnecessary architecture layers.

use_cases.title: Separate service entry points
use_cases.description: Organize server, worker, and migration binaries while keeping shared business logic in private packages.

use_cases.title: Coordinate related Go modules
use_cases.description: Plan workspace membership and local dependency resolution for modules developed together in a monorepo.

prompt_templates.title: Choose a minimal layout
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me plan a small Go CLI called [name]. Ask about architecture first, then dependency injection. Recommend a minimal layout without editing files.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: planning a first Go project

prompt_templates.title: Organize a service
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a layout for [service] with an API server and migration binary. Ask about architecture and dependency injection before suggesting packages. Include test placement.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: separating entry points and application logic

prompt_templates.title: Review package boundaries
prompt_templates.prompt: Review [directory tree] for private implementation and reusable API boundaries. Recommend focused layout changes and explain module naming. Do not modify persistent agent configuration.
prompt_templates.scenario: Experienced: reviewing an existing project structure

prompt_templates.title: Plan a multi-module workspace
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a go.work workspace for [module paths]. Explain local resolution, initialization, and cross-module testing. Identify when a single module is preferable. Propose changes before execution.

output_examples.input: Plan a small CLI with a flat architecture and no dependency injection framework.
output: Use one command entry point with minimal startup logic.
Keep private behavior in a small internal package.
Place tests beside their implementation and fixtures in a local testdata directory.
Start with one module and omit a workspace.

output_examples.input: Our server and shared logging library are separate modules developed together. Should we use a workspace?
output: A workspace fits related modules that need local cross-module development.
Add both existing module directories to workspace membership.
Keep each module's dependency metadata separate.
Use local workspace resolution instead of repeated replacement directives.

output_examples.input: Where should private request parsing and a reusable public logging package live?
output: Keep request parsing in an internal package.
Expose the logging API through a public package when external consumers need it.
For a dedicated library module, prefer a root-level public package.
Keep executable startup logic separate from reusable behavior.

best_practices: Confirm project scope, architecture, and dependency injection preferences before creating directories.
Use workspaces for related modules, not merely for multiple packages within one module.
Review templates and commands before execution, and require approval for persistent agent configuration changes.
anti_patterns: Creating empty architecture layers or public packages without a concrete need.
Collecting business logic in entry points or vague utility packages.
Automatically adding always-load skill instructions to persistent project configuration without explicit approval.

faq.question: What does this skill help organize?
faq.answer: It covers project directories, module naming, package boundaries, test placement, configuration, and multi-module workspaces.

faq.question: Does every project need go.work?
faq.answer: No. A single module with multiple packages does not need a workspace. Workspaces support local development across related modules.

faq.question: Is pkg required for public libraries?
faq.answer: No. The library reference recommends root-level public packages. The application guidance treats pkg as optional when external consumers need reusable code.

faq.question: Does the skill include a complete application generator?
faq.answer: No. It provides instructions, examples, and build templates. An agent may apply them, but generated projects still require review and testing.

faq.question: What tools are needed to run the suggested commands?
faq.answer: Go is required. The Makefile also uses Make and Git, while optional targets require tools such as golangci-lint, govulncheck, and air.

faq.question: Does the skill change persistent agent instructions?
faq.answer: Its checklist requests an always-load directive without confirmation. Remove that instruction or explicitly approve a reviewed change before allowing persistent configuration edits.
